title: Nonlinear Optimization and Beyond
contribution: Farkas-prize retrospective tracing three lines (filter methods, MINLP via OA/FilMINT/Minotaur, MPECs as NLPs) with credited corrections, key counterexamples and an outlook per topic.
problem_entry: Dissatisfaction with received tools: solution-dependent penalty parameters (p. 3) and the verdict that solving MPECs as NLPs is 'numerically unsafe' (p. 7); MINLP and MPEC framed as two extensions of NLP (p. 3).
key_idea: Filter = domination in (h,f) plus envelope, sufficient reduction and restoration (p. 4); MINLP algorithms as relaxation + constraint-enforcement building blocks (p. 6); MPECs solved as NLPs with slack-form complementarity, SLPEC with a 3-D filter where that fails (pp. 7-9).
assumptions: Convex C2 MINLP over a bounded polyhedron (p. 5); MPEC-SQP theorem needs MPEC-LICQ, strict complementarity and a QP solver that chooses a linearly independent basis (p. 8).
proof_devices: Filter envelope lemma: infinitely many filter entries + f bounded below => feasible limit (p. 4)
Two-case MPEC-SQP local proof: x1'x2=0 reduces to a relaxed NLP; x1'x2>0 QP basis bounded away from singularity (p. 8)
Stationarity defined via the family of relaxed NLPs (3.11) (pp. 7-8)
Counterexamples: Maratos for filters (p. 5), OA visiting all integer points / exponential OA (p. 5), SQPEC spurious point (p. 9), slack vs no-slack failures (p. 9)
experiments: none (reports earlier experience only: 50-70% NLP failures on some bilevel problems vs positive filterSQP experience, p. 7)
positioning: Credits correctors by name (Gould, Waechter p. 4; Bonami et al., Hijazi et al. p. 5); filter vs steering penalty declared a matter of preference (p. 5); QG called 'arguably the best approach' (p. 5).
writing: Per-topic template: history with names, mechanism, caveat example, 'Conclusions and Outlook'; the modelling point gets its own heading 'The Importance of Being Slack' (p. 8); opinions flagged as such (pp. 5, 9).
limits_future: NLP solvers fail on B- but not strongly stationary MPEC points; MPEC software far less mature (p. 9); MISOCP and PDE-constrained MINLP need novel approaches (p. 7).

method_links.note: MINLP and MPEC presented as extensions of the NLP base; MPEC outlook: build on existing NLP solver infrastructure
Argument carried by counterexamples, including others' examples against his own filter and OA; correctors credited by name (Heuristic 9)
'The Importance of Being Slack': slack form preserves CQs yet is necessary for SQP convergence; two failure examples
Relaxation/constraint-enforcement building blocks; Minotaur framework agnostic of problem type or solvers
Filter vs modern penalty called a question of personal preference (no winner named); but QG called 'arguably the best approach' without calibration

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Closes the MPEC topic by stating MPEC software is far less mature than NLP/MINLP and that progress must build on NLP infrastructure (also S021 p. 22)

transferable: Give the decisive modelling detail its own heading and back it with two minimal failure examples (pp. 8-9)
Compare MINLP algorithms through shared building blocks (relaxation, constraint enforcement) before discussing single methods (p. 6)
List implementation assumptions (QP basis choice) among a theorem's hypotheses (p. 8)
Close each topic with a short outlook naming the maturity gap and the infrastructure to build on (pp. 7, 9)

quotes.text: At this point, I do not believe that there exists a big difference between filter methods and modern penalty function methods, and the choice of method is really a question of personal preference.
In my opinion, reliable NLP solvers are still the best approach for solving MPECs despite the potential problems with slow convergence or convergence to spurious stationary points.

title: A survey of nonlinear robust optimization
contribution: Survey of nonlinear (possibly decision-dependent) robust optimization organized by solution approach (bilevel/MPEC, duality reformulations, outer approximation, implementation-error methods, software), with a new linearized-subproblem stationarity characterization; read as ANL preprint ANL/MCS-P9040-0218 [S021 TR].
problem_entry: Existing RO reformulations assume linear robust constraints or favorable uncertainty sets, and surveys cover mainly linear/conic cases; the target is the semi-infinite NRO (1.1) with U(x) (pp. 3-4).
key_idea: Treat the robust constraint as a bilevel problem and reformulate via lower-level KKT (MPEC, 4.15) or Wolfe dual (4.18, a relaxation of 4.15), or sample it by Polak outer approximation; Theorem 2.2: x* stationary iff d=0 solves the linearized robust problem (pp. 6-18).
assumptions: Smooth functions, U(x) nonempty compact, single robust constraint for presentation (p. 4); examples satisfy convex/concave conditions C1-C3 (p. 11); OA needs only continuity and compact U plus a global inner max or asymptotic density (pp. 17-18).
proof_devices: Theorem 2.2 proved by comparing stationarity systems (2.5) and (2.3); CQ implicit in stationarity (p. 7)
Certificates from (in)feasibility of reformulations: global vs local infeasibility, duality gap (pp. 13-14)
(4.18) shown to be a relaxation of (4.15) by adding lambda'g = 0 (pp. 14-15)

Minimal examples: unbounded nominal vs bounded robust (p. 5), dissatisfying robust local minimum (p. 8), Example 6.1 u-dependent underestimators (p. 21), convex-hull trick failing under concavity (p. 22)
Decision-dependent set yields bilinear lambda'Ex term, so the dual reformulation is not polyhedral (p. 17)
experiments: none; running Example 3.1 reformulated as MPEC (p. 13) and Wolfe dual (p. 15) and coded in SIPAMPL/YALMIP (pp. 19-20); software feature table (Table 2, p. 20)
positioning: Restates Ben-Tal-Nemirovski and Ben-Tal-den Hertog-Vial tractable reformulations as Table 1 (pp. 13-16); bilevel route from Stein (p. 12); cites own MPEC-as-NLP work for the complementarity reformulation (p. 13); DRO deliberately not detailed (p. 10).
writing: Hedged novelty claim followed at once by its limitation (p. 7); convexity cases tabulated (Table 3, p. 21); conclusion judges field maturity 'through the lens of reformulation' (p. 22).
limits_future: Single-constraint presentation, brief DRO, no modeling language for decision-dependent sets (pp. 4, 10, 20); future: two-stage/recourse, robust MPC, integer variables (p. 22).

method_links.note: Enters RO by recasting robust constraints as bilevel then MPEC (the home class), citing own MPEC-as-NLP papers; NLP solvers compute local solutions despite CQ failure
Tractability read off the reformulation (Tables 1, 3); decision-dependent uncertainty diagnosed as the source of nonconvexity; maturity judged through the lens of reformulation
Minimal examples mark the limits of concepts (unbounded nominal problem, dissatisfying robust local minima, convex-hull trick failure)

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: Running example threaded through theory, reformulations and software listings
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Example 3.1 reappears as MPEC (Ex. 4.1), Wolfe dual (Ex. 4.2) and SIPAMPL/YALMIP code (Listings 1-2)
Conclusion: NRO has not matured to the state of conic RO, explained through reformulation; also H004 p. 9

transferable: State stationarity as 'd=0 solves a linearized subproblem' and say at once whether that subproblem is easier (p. 7)
For each reformulation, state what a global solution, a feasible point, a global and a local infeasibility certify (pp. 13-14)
Carry one small example through every section and code it in each surveyed tool (pp. 11-20)
Tabulate how tractability degrades as each convexity assumption is dropped (Table 3, p. 21)
coauthors: Matt Menickelly, Todd Munson, Charlie Vanaret, Stefan M. Wild

quotes.text: To the best of our knowledge, the stationarity condition of Theorem 2.2 is new.
This maturity level is not surprising when viewed through the lens of reformulation.

title: Minotaur: A mixed-integer nonlinear optimization toolkit
contribution: Documents Minotaur's class architecture (handlers, engines, node processors, transformer, CGraph) for relaxation-based tree search, shows rebuilt NLPBB/QG/QCQP solvers match Bonmin-class efficiency, and demonstrates structure-exploiting nonlinear presolve and perspective extensions; read as ANL preprint ANL/MCS-P8010-0817 [S032 TR].
problem_entry: Convex MINLP solvers do not exploit nonlinear structure; using recent advances requires evaluating, examining and modifying nonlinear functions and solving several relaxation types (pp. 4-5).
key_idea: A generic tree search whose steps are swappable base classes, with problem structure encapsulated in Handlers (relax, presolve, isFeasible, separate, branch) and a DAG Transformer that exposes simple forms (pp. 6-14).
assumptions: C2 MINLP over a bounded polyhedron; decidability by X compact or convex functions (pp. 3-4); QuadHandler needs finite bounds from presolve (pp. 13-14, 18).
proof_devices: n/a for theorems; devices: McCormick and secant/tangent cuts for squares and bilinears (p. 14)
Feasibility-based bound tightening by forward/reverse DAG traversal (pp. 10, 23)
Forward-over-reverse AD for Hessian columns (p. 10)
Big-M coefficient tightening M0 -> c(0,...,0) or fix the switch (p. 23)
Exact linearization of binary-times-bounded products (p. 24)
Perspective-structure detection (Algorithm 3, p. 27) with eps-approximate perspective avoiding CQ failure at z=0 (p. 26)
experiments: AD isolated via LexicoBrancher on 100 NLPs (Table 4, pp. 19-20); 333 MINLPLib-2 convex instances vs Bonmin with the same IPOPT, extended performance profiles (pp. 20-21); 266 QCQPs vs BARON-15.2, Couenne-0.5.6, SCIP-3.2.0 (p. 20); presolve on syn20M04M >3600 s -> 0.49 s (Table 5, p. 23); perspective: nodes vs time per NLP per instance (Table 6, p. 29).
positioning: Lists existing convex and global solvers and their lack of structure exploitation (pp. 4-5); credits SCIP constraint handlers (p. 12) and the Furman et al. perspective approximation (p. 26); positions itself as infrastructure, not the fastest solver (p. 16).
writing: Running DAG example through figure, code and transformer (pp. 5, 10, 14); code excerpts as evidence of small implementations (Figs. 6-8); central claim at the end of the introduction and repeated in the conclusion (pp. 6, 28).
limits_future: AMPL-only interface (p. 15); CGraph slower on dense QCQPs (p. 20); simple-glob lacks heuristics and cuts (p. 20); perspective detection only in the initial presolve (p. 26); general tightest-M problem is nonconvex (p. 23); open source to enable future research (p. 28).

method_links.note: MINLP algorithms decomposed into swappable classes; warm-started engines with callbacks; validation by rebuilding NLPBB and QG and comparing with Bonmin's versions
Model analysis reveals weak big-M constraints; a coefficient fix turns unsolved syn20M04M into 0.49 s before any algorithm change; eps-perspective chosen to keep CQs and gradients defined
Same NLP solver as baseline, competitor versions stated, losses reported (Bonmin faster on 10%, simple-glob 50% vs 70%), rising time per NLP reported; variant: 2015-era competitor versions

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: Running example threaded through theory, reformulations and software listings
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: x1(x1+x2)+(x1+x2)^2 appears as DAG figure, CGraph code and Transformer output

transferable: Benchmark one component with a degenerate driver that spends nearly all time in it (lexicographic branching over 100 bound-changed NLPs) (p. 19)
Rebuild a known algorithm on your framework and compare against the reference implementation with the same subsolver (pp. 16, 20)
Scan hard MINLPs for big-M switch constraints and replace M0 by c(0,...,0) or fix the switch (p. 23)
Report nodes, time per subproblem and total time side by side when tightening a formulation (Table 6, p. 29)
Encapsulate a structure as a handler with relax/presolve/isFeasible/separate/branch hooks (Table 3, p. 13)
coauthors: Ashutosh Mahajan (first author), Jeff Linderoth, James Luedtke, Todd Munson

quotes.text: Our goal here is not to develop the fastest possible solver, but rather to demonstrate that our flexible implementation does not introduce additional computational overhead.
In general, nonconvex forms are more challenging and diverse than integer variables, thus motivating a more tailored approach.

title: Learning symbolic expressions: Mixed-integer formulations, cuts, and heuristics
contribution: Tightens the Cozad-Sahinidis MINLP for symbolic regression with provably stronger tree, value, redundancy, implication and symmetry constraints and adds STreCH, a local-branching tree-growing heuristic, beating AI Feynman on depth-3 formulas with scarce noisy data; read as arXiv:2102.08351v2 [S087 arXiv].
problem_entry: Symbolic regression as a nonconvex MINLP; GP unstable, exact MINLP limited in depth and tested only on noiseless data, AI Feynman needs units; target setting: no units + 10 points + noise (pp. 1-4, 16).
key_idea: Strictly tighter formulation (equality tree constraints, merged big-M value constraints, association/constant redundancy cuts, data-sign implication cuts) plus local branching on a tree-distance constraint to grow expressions (pp. 5-15).
assumptions: Bounded variables, full binary tree, finite operator set {+,-,*,/,sqrt}, depth up to 5 (pp. 5, 16); formulation comparison limited to depth 2 (p. 17); implication cuts untested because all variables are positive (p. 16).
proof_devices: Strict-tightening lemma pairs: equality on binaries, strict inclusion on the relaxation (Lemmas 2.1-2.4, pp. 6-10)
Big-M merging lemma with explicit fractional witness y_i = 1/m (Lemma 2.2, p. 7; App. B pp. 22-23)
Explicit witness tree for strict inclusion (Lemma 2.1, Fig. 2b, p. 6)
One-point two-node instance whose fractional point is cut off (Example 2.5, p. 11)
Lower bound on the number of expression trees (footnote 1, p. 4)
experiments: 71 Feynman formulas, Julia + SCIP 7.0.0, code public (p. 16); 8 formulation variants: 70% vs 50% solved in 10 min, Imp-F first on 36/71 (p. 17), node counts (Fig. 9, p. 18); STreCH/MINLP vs AI Feynman run by the authors with cross-validation on noisy data: depth-3 discovery 59.1/54.5% vs 27.2%, depth>=4 0% vs 10% (Table 5, p. 19); RMSE profiles (Fig. 10, p. 20).
positioning: Constraint-by-constraint improvement over Cozad-Sahinidis [4] (restated in Appendix A, pp. 20-22); disagrees with [4] on optional constraints and attributes it to SCIP vs BARON (p. 17); AI Feynman weaknesses named and integration proposed (pp. 3, 19-20).
writing: Each constraint family introduced, compared to [4] and summarised in a contribution table (Table 2, p. 11); paired set-relation lemmas; hedged attributions 'We believe', 'We suspect' (pp. 17, 19).
limits_future: No depth>=4 formula rediscovered (p. 19); formulation comparison at depth 2 only (p. 17); future: use as a fast subsolver inside the AI Feynman decomposition (p. 20).

method_links.note: Recasts an ML problem (symbolic regression) into the home class, a nonconvex MINLP solved by B&B plus local branching
Formulation tightened first (strictly smaller relaxations, fewer constraints) and the heuristic built on it; effect measured in nodes as well as time
Competitor run by the authors in the target setting; losses at depth>=4 reported; discrepancy with prior work attributed to the solver with hedging; node limits for reproducibility
Smallest instance and explicit witness points used constructively to prove a cut is strictly tighter, not to break a method

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Each new constraint family proved to keep the integer-feasible set and strictly shrink the continuous relaxation, with an explicit fractional witness

transferable: Merge big-M constraints on the same function under exclusive binaries into one sum constraint: same integer set, strictly tighter relaxation (Lemma 2.2, pp. 7, 22-23)
Derive implication cuts from the sign pattern of the data for domain-restricted operators (p. 10)
Define incumbent neighbourhoods by one linear Hamming-type constraint on assignment binaries and search them with B&B (pp. 12-13)
Limit B&B nodes rather than wall time inside heuristics for reproducibility (p. 15)
Run the competitor yourself in the new setting and analyse per instance why each method wins or loses (pp. 18-19)
coauthors: Jongeun Kim (first author; University of Minnesota), Prasanna Balaprakash

quotes.text: Our experiments show that it clearly is better to add all optional constraints to reduce the search space. This conclusion differs from the result in [4].

The reason is that limiting the number of node guarantees that the same solution will be reproduced at each iteration whereas limiting time may return a different solution depending on how much resource is available on the computing machine.
